newsitem.title: EGYPT: Analysts say Hebron deal does not ensure more deals.
newsitem.headline: Analysts say Hebron deal does not ensure more deals.

text.p: The deal Israel made with the Palestinians to expand self-rule in Hebron eases pressure on the Jewish state to move forward on other Middle East peace tracks, analysts and diplomats said on Thursday.
"Israel's having a deal on Hebron would benefit (Israel) by breaking off the international pressure which was building on it on Hebron," said a senior Arab official in Cairo.
"It takes off the heat. Israel would now not feel the need anymore to have the peace process on the front burner. We are going to have a no peace, no war situation," he said.

Analysts said they did not expect Israeli willingness to redeploy in Hebron to spill over into any breakthrough with Lebanon, where Israel occupies a border strip, or with Syria in negotiations on the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights. The talks between Syria and Israel broke off last March.

Israeli and Palestinian negotiators, pushed hard by the United States, this week agreed on the long-delayed deal to launch self-rule in Hebron, located in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. They also agreed on a timetable for Israeli withdrawals from other parts of the West Bank.

But the slow pace of the talks angered Arab states, which saw Israel's reluctance to redeploy troops as a sign it was ignoring peace deals already made between Palestinians and the government that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ousted in May.
Israel's parliament on Thursday was due to vote on the accord, which was already approved by the cabinet despite opposition from hardline ministers.
But some Arab officials think that the deal heralds movement on other peace tracks.
A diplomat whose country was close to the talks on Hebron said: "It's a good deal. We hope for a comprehensive continuation of the peace process now on the Lebanese and Syrian tracks."
Israeli-Syrian negotiations, held only intermittently since they started in 1991, are frozen over the future of the Golan Heights, captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war.
Policy guidelines of Netanyahu's Likud party say Israel must maintain sovereignty over the strategic plateau.
On Wednesday, Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak offered his congratulations and King Hussein of Jordan said he was happy about the Hebron deal, to which they both gave proposals.
Jordanian Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti, asked on Monday whether he thought the Hebron negotiations represented a softening of Israel's position, said: "Very much so."
Syrian Foreign Minister Farouq al-Shara said in Cairo last month that Syria would welcome new peace talks with Israel, provided they resumed where they broke off in 1996.
But he said Israel must give a commitment to withdraw from all the Golan Heights.

Shara said according to one theory Israel was interested in improving its government's image abroad. "The other theory is that after finishing off the question of Hebron, Israel will go into a serious process towards resuming negotiations on all tracks, that is on the Syrian and Lebanese tracks," he said.
Syria's official Tishreen newspaper, virtually brushing off the importance of the Hebron deal, said on Thursday it saw no signs of Israeli willingness to further peace.
"Had Israeli leaders been interested in peace and stability in the region they would have announced their acceptance of U.N. resolutions and the land-for-peace principle," it said.
"What Israeli leaders are declaring is contrary to that. They are saying no to withdrawal from the Golan and south Lebanon. No to Palestinian rights. No to termination of settlement building."
